citation: Md. Code Ann., Econ. Dev. §§14-301 to 14-302 (Title 14, Subtitle 3; enacted by 2015 Md. Laws, ch. 164 [SB 370], "Unmanned Aircraft Systems Research, Development, Regulation, and Privacy Act of 2015"; no subsequent amendment identified in the current codified text)

summary: Md. Code Ann., Econ. Dev. §14-301, enacted by the Unmanned Aircraft Systems Research, Development, Regulation, and Privacy Act of 2015 (2015 Md. Laws, ch. 164 [SB 370]), provides that only the State may enact a law or take other action to prohibit, restrict, or regulate the testing or operation of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) in Maryland; subsection (c) expressly preempts county and municipal authority to do so and supersedes any existing local ordinance that prohibits, restricts, or regulates UAS testing or operation, without affecting federal preemption of state law (subsection (d)). A companion section, §14-302, requires the Department (Commerce) and the Maryland Department of Transportation, including the Maryland Aviation Administration (MDOT MAA), to monitor FAA UAS rulemaking, assess its impact on the State, consult with the University of Maryland's Mid-Atlantic Aviation Partnership and local governments, and report findings and recommendations to the Governor and General Assembly.

This claim should be treated as unverified pending review of the 2015 session's full chaptered bill text. Multiple Maryland counties (Carroll, Frederick, Montgomery, St. Mary's) reportedly maintain park-permit or drone ordinances arguably in tension with this preemption provision (see printable summary, Non-Regulatory Context) — a live, unresolved compliance ambiguity for AEC operators, since local officials and the Maryland Attorney General's office have publicly avoided taking a firm position on which law controls.

summary: Md. Code Ann., Crim. Law §9-417.1, enacted by 2024 Md. Laws, ch. 101 (SB 273), makes it unlawful for a person to deliver contraband to a person detained or confined in a place of confinement using an unmanned aircraft (defined as an aircraft operated without the possibility of direct human intervention from within or on the aircraft). A violation is a misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment not exceeding 3 years, a fine not exceeding $1,000, or both. Every correctional facility must post exterior signage warning of the section's provisions in an area visible to the general public.

Laws, ch. 101) directly.

summary: Md. Code Ann., Nat. Res. §10-410(j) makes it unlawful for a person to hunt or attempt to hunt wild birds or mammals from an aircraft within Maryland; a violation is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not exceeding $1,000, imprisonment not exceeding 6 months, or both, with costs imposed in the court's discretion. "Aircraft" is not separately defined within §10-410 itself. Numerous secondary drone-law compilations describe additional, more granular DNR-published restrictions specific to unmanned aircraft — including a bar on using a drone to locate, drive, or flush game, a 24-hour gap required between drone-based scouting and hunting the same property, and a wounded/expired-game recovery exception conditioned on notifying the Natural Resources Police — but this research pass could not independently open and verify the specific COMAR provision or DNR Guide to Hunting and Trapping page stating those rules.

summary: DNR's "Statewide Maryland Park Policies" webpage states that UAS operated on land owned and managed by the Department of Natural Resources, including state parks, must comply with all FAA regulations and all State and federal law, including the Use of State Parks regulations, and that every drone operator must contact the Park Manager before flying in a State Park to ensure the operation does not jeopardize public safety or park resources. Individual parks may set park-specific conditions; for example, Sandy Point State Park permits drone operation only before the Memorial Day holiday and after the Labor Day holiday, during normal park operating hours, subject to FAA compliance and restrictions near the adjacent Chesapeake Bay Bridge.

summary: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §15-101(k) defines "practice land surveying" to include, among other listed activities, "utilizing measurement devices or systems, such as aerial photogrammetry, global positioning systems, land information systems, geographic information systems, or similar technology for evaluation or location of boundaries of real property, easements, or rights-of-way." The definition also covers measuring, platting, and locating lines, angles, elevations, and natural or artificial features "in the air, on the surface of the earth, in underground work, and on the beds of bodies of water." No standalone State Board for Professional Land Surveyors rule, advisory opinion, or FAQ specifically addressing UAS-derived photogrammetric or LiDAR survey deliverables was located during this research pass.

No enacted Maryland statute imposing a state-agency UAS procurement, approved-manufacturer, or country-of-origin restriction was located (a federal restriction under the American Security Drone Act took effect for federally funded contracts in December 2025, but this is a federal, not state, requirement). Pursuant to 2015 Md. Laws, ch. 164, §5, the Maryland Department of State Police and MDOT MAA submitted a joint report on UAS in Maryland to the Governor and General Assembly on December 17, 2018, documenting recreational/commercial UAS registration data, reported incidents, and a working-group recommendation to allow the federal regulatory framework to mature rather than pursue additional state legislation at that time. Separately, HB0471 (2026 Regular Session), sponsored by Del. Robin Grammer Jr. and titled "Public Safety – State and Local Governments – Use of Unmanned Aircraft," would require a warrant for most state/local government UAS surveillance, render improperly obtained UAS evidence inadmissible, and restrict UAS deployment by government units; as of this research date it remains pending in the House Judiciary Committee (hearing held Feb. 24, 2026) and was previously introduced without enactment as HB0954 in the 2025 Regular Session.
